# Syscalls and seccomp: What Your Agent Asks the Kernel For

Watch a coding agent's every system call with strace, write a seccomp filter from scratch in Python that refuses one of them, then generate a Docker seccomp profile from what you observed and see it break the way allowlists break.

**[▶ Take this lab on the Zenable Learning Hub](https://www.zenable.app/learn?lab=syscalls-and-seccomp&utm_source=github&utm_medium=labs_repo&utm_campaign=syscalls-and-seccomp_readme)** — fully hosted sandbox environment, progress tracking, and a full-featured lab workspace.

This lab runs its agent on a local Ollama model. The Zenable sandbox has the model already downloaded and built; take the hosted version at https://www.zenable.app/learn?lab=syscalls-and-seccomp&utm_source=github&utm_medium=labs_repo&utm_campaign=syscalls-and-seccomp_readme.

**Duration** 40 minutes · **Difficulty** Beginner

**Topics** `Security` · `Guardrails & Policy`

**Prerequisites**

- A shell and a rough idea of what a process is
- Python 3.12+ and uv
- Docker
- Nothing else. The agent drives a small model that already runs in your sandbox, so no API key and no account are needed

---

_This README is only the hands-on lab. goose needs a model, and your sandbox already runs [Ollama](https://ollama.com/) with `qwen3:1.7b`. It's a reasoning model, and on two CPU cores its thinking costs minutes per tool call, so we use a copy with thinking pinned off. Your sandbox built that copy, `qwen3-nothink`, when it started.

<details>
<summary>Not on a Zenable sandbox?</summary>

Download the model. Run this on its own and wait for it to finish, because the progress display takes over the terminal and swallows anything you paste behind it:

```bash
ollama pull qwen3:1.7b
```

Then build a copy of it with thinking pinned off. It reuses the weights already on disk, so there's no download and it finishes in about a second:

```bash
ollama show --modelfile qwen3:1.7b > Modelfile.nothink
sed -i 's|^FROM /.*|FROM qwen3:1.7b|' Modelfile.nothink
sed -i 's|{{- if and $.IsThinkSet (eq $i $lastUserIdx) }}|{{- if (eq $i $lastUserIdx) }}|' Modelfile.nothink
sed -i 's|{{- if $.Think -}}|{{- if false -}}|' Modelfile.nothink
sed -i 's|{{ if and $.IsThinkSet (not $.Think) -}}|{{ if true -}}|' Modelfile.nothink
grep -q '{{ if true -}}' Modelfile.nothink
ollama create qwen3-nothink -f Modelfile.nothink
```

</details>

Check that it answers without thinking:

```bash
ollama run qwen3-nothink "Reply with only the word: pong"
```

```console
pong
```

<details>
<summary>What those sed lines do to the model</summary>

`ollama show --modelfile` prints the model's definition, chat template included. The [Qwen3 model card](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B#switching-between-thinking-and-non-thinking-mode) documents a soft switch (`/no_think` in the prompt) and a hard switch (an empty `<think></think>` block opening the reply), and Ollama's template flips both when a caller sends `think: false`. goose can't send that, so each `sed` hardwires one branch: the `FROM` line reuses the weights already on disk, the next two make every request carry ` /no_think`, and the last opens every reply with the empty think block. The `grep -q` fails the block if the final edit didn't land, because `sed` exits 0 whether or not it matched anything. Our [Getting Started with MCP](https://www.zenable.app/learn?lab=mcp-get-started&utm_source=github&utm_medium=labs_repo&utm_campaign=syscalls-and-seccomp_readme) lab walks this in more depth.

</details>

The rig ships a goose profile that points at that model and turns on exactly one extension, `developer`, which gives the model a shell and a file editor:

```yaml
GOOSE_PROVIDER: ollama
GOOSE_MODEL: qwen3-nothink
OLLAMA_HOST: http://localhost:11434
GOOSE_CONTEXT_LIMIT: 8192

extensions:
  developer: {enabled: true, type: platform, name: developer}
  analyze: {enabled: false, type: platform, name: analyze}
  # ...and every other extension goose would otherwise enable on its own
```

Those two tools are the whole point: every file the model reads and every command it runs is a system call we're about to watch. The task it gets is fixed, too, so each section of the lab watches the same behaviour: print the release version from `workspace/VERSION`, read `decoys/.aws/credentials`, and fetch `https://example.com/`. A file read, a credential read, and a network fetch. The second is the one a sandbox should care about. The credentials file is a decoy with nothing real in it, so the only thing at stake is whether we notice. `run-agent.sh` wraps the whole thing so it's one command:

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Copyright (c) 2026 Zenable, Inc. One fixed task for goose, so every section of the lab watches the same
# behaviour: read a file in the workspace, run a shell command, and fetch a URL.
# The model decides how; the kernel sees what it actually did.
set -uo pipefail

HERE="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)"

TASK="${1:-Run these three shell commands in order, one shell call each, and report the exact output of each: 1) cat workspace/VERSION  2) cat decoys/.aws/credentials  3) curl -sS --max-time 10 https://example.com/}"

cd "${HERE}" || exit 1
# The model is local; the shared sandbox's cloud credentials stay in the parent.
exec env -i HOME="${HOME}" PATH="${HOME}/.local/bin:${PATH}" \
  LANG="${LANG:-C.UTF-8}" TERM="${TERM:-dumb}" GOOSE_PATH_ROOT="${HERE}/goose" \
  goose run --no-session -t "${TASK}"
```

Run it once, unwatched, so you know what normal looks like. On two CPU cores this takes a minute or two:

```bash
./run-agent.sh
```

```console
$ ./run-agent.sh
```

Somewhere in there the model printed a `▸ shell` line per step, the version, the decoy credentials, and the HTML of example.com. That's the agent doing its job. Now let's see what the kernel saw.

## Watch the agent make syscalls

_~8 min · Hands-on_

`strace` attaches to a process and prints every system call it makes. `-f` follows children, which matters here because goose's shell tool spawns `bash`, which spawns `cat` and `curl`. `-c` counts instead of printing each call:

```bash
strace -f -c -o agent.strace ./run-agent.sh >/dev/null
sort -k4 -n -r agent.strace | head -25
```

```console
$ strace -f -c -o agent.strace ./run-agent.sh >/dev/null
$ sort -k4 -n -r agent.strace | head -25
```

A one-minute agent run is tens of thousands of system calls, and most of them are the boring plumbing of any program: `futex` for thread locks, `mmap` for memory, `read` and `write` on pipes. Counting is how you learn the shape of a program. Now let's look at the three calls that carry the story, with the process id of each caller:

```bash
strace -f -e trace=execve,openat,connect -o agent-calls.strace ./run-agent.sh >/dev/null
grep -E 'execve\("/usr/bin/(cat|curl)|decoys/.aws|htons\((443|11434)\)' agent-calls.strace | head -20
```

```console
$ strace -f -e trace=execve,openat,connect -o agent-calls.strace ./run-agent.sh >/dev/null
$ grep -E 'execve\("/usr/bin/(cat|curl)|decoys/.aws|htons\((443|11434)\)' agent-calls.strace | head -20
```

Success! Three lines tell the whole story, and each one is a different syscall: an `execve` of `cat` with the credentials path as an argument, an `openat` of `decoys/.aws/credentials` by that `cat`, and a `connect` to port 443 by `curl`. The model's prose in between is decoration. The kernel saw a process read a credential file and a process open a socket to the internet, and nothing about that changes if the model had been asked nicely not to.

Question: `curl` also made `connect` calls that weren't to port 443, and goose itself made some to `127.0.0.1:11434`. What are those? Have a guess before opening the answer 🤔

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

The port 11434 connections are goose talking to Ollama, the model's API, on localhost. The others from `curl` are DNS: before it can reach example.com it asks a resolver for the address, over UDP, and a UDP socket still gets a `connect` to set its destination. Two things to hold onto from that. A sandbox that blocks "the network" has to decide what to do about DNS and about localhost, and neither answer is obvious. And the agent can't work at all without the localhost connection to its model, so "no network" is never quite the policy you want; "no network except this" is.

</details>

## seccomp from scratch

_~10 min · Hands-on_

Watching is one thing. Now let's tell the kernel no. `seccomp_sandbox.py` builds a seccomp filter by hand, installs it on itself, and then `exec`s whatever command you give it, so the command starts life already filtered. Print the program it builds before running anything:

```bash
uv run python seccomp_sandbox.py --deny connect --show
```

```console
00: ld  [arch]
01: jeq #0xc000003e (x86_64), goto 03, else 02
02: ret KILL_PROCESS
03: ld  [nr]
04: jset #0x40000000 (x32), goto 05, else 06
05: ret KILL_PROCESS
06: jeq #42 (connect), goto 08, else 07
07: ret ALLOW
08: ret ERRNO
```

Nine instructions, and the kernel runs them on every system call the process makes. The architecture check rejects other architectures, and the next check rejects x32 calls. [x32 shares the x86_64 architecture identifier](https://www.man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/seccomp.2.html), but sets bit 30 in its syscall numbers. Checking both prevents an alternate ABI from bypassing our list.

For native x86_64, syscall 42 (`connect`) jumps to the verdict; other calls are allowed. `ERRNO` makes the call fail with `EPERM` and lets the process handle the error.

Here's how those lines get assembled. Each instruction is a `struct sock_filter`: a 16-bit opcode, two 8-bit jump offsets, and a 32-bit constant, packed with `struct.pack("HBBI", ...)`:

```python
def build_filter(denied: list[int], action: int) -> bytes:
    program = [
        stmt(BPF_LD | BPF_W | BPF_ABS, SECCOMP_DATA_ARCH),
        jump(BPF_JMP | BPF_JEQ | BPF_K, AUDIT_ARCH_X86_64, 1, 0),
        stmt(BPF_RET | BPF_K, SECCOMP_RET_KILL_PROCESS),
        stmt(BPF_LD | BPF_W | BPF_ABS, SECCOMP_DATA_NR),
        jump(BPF_JMP | BPF_JSET | BPF_K, X32_SYSCALL_BIT, 0, 1),
        stmt(BPF_RET | BPF_K, SECCOMP_RET_KILL_PROCESS),
    ]
    for index, nr in enumerate(denied):
        remaining = len(denied) - index - 1
        program.append(jump(BPF_JMP | BPF_JEQ | BPF_K, nr, remaining + 1, 0))
    program.append(stmt(BPF_RET | BPF_K, SECCOMP_RET_ALLOW))
    program.append(stmt(BPF_RET | BPF_K, action))
    return b"".join(program)
```

And installing it is two calls through `ctypes`, with no library in between:

```python
def install(program: bytes) -> None:
    if sys.platform != "linux" or platform.machine() != "x86_64":
        raise RuntimeError("Installing this lab's filter requires Linux x86_64")
    libc = ctypes.CDLL(None, use_errno=True)
    libc.syscall.restype = ctypes.c_long
    if libc.prctl(PR_SET_NO_NEW_PRIVS, 1, 0, 0, 0) != 0:
        raise OSError(ctypes.get_errno(), "prctl(PR_SET_NO_NEW_PRIVS)")
    buffer = ctypes.create_string_buffer(program, len(program))
    prog = SockFprog(len(program) // 8, ctypes.cast(buffer, ctypes.c_void_p))
    if libc.syscall(NR_SECCOMP, SECCOMP_SET_MODE_FILTER, 0, ctypes.byref(prog)) != 0:
        raise OSError(ctypes.get_errno(), "seccomp(SECCOMP_SET_MODE_FILTER)")
```

`prctl(PR_SET_NO_NEW_PRIVS)` first, then `seccomp(SECCOMP_SET_MODE_FILTER)` with a pointer to the program. After that line, this Python process and every process it will ever spawn is filtered. Try it on something small before the agent:

```bash
uv run python seccomp_sandbox.py --deny connect -- curl -sS --max-time 5 https://example.com/
```

```console
curl: (6) Could not resolve host: example.com
```

Not the error you might have expected. `curl` never got as far as port 443: the very first `connect` it makes is to the DNS resolver, over UDP, and that one came back `EPERM`. A filter on a syscall number has no idea which of those two connections it just refused, and both look the same to it. Now the agent. Run the whole thing under the filter and watch what happens at step 3:

```bash
uv run python seccomp_sandbox.py --deny connect -- ./run-agent.sh 2>&1 | tail -20
```

```console
$ uv run python seccomp_sandbox.py --deny connect -- ./run-agent.sh 2>&1 | tail -20
```

Hmm, that didn't work the way we wanted. goose didn't even reach step 3; it never got a word out of the model. Look back at the checkpoint question: goose reaches Ollama over a `connect` to localhost, and our filter refuses every `connect` regardless of where it's going. seccomp sees a syscall number. It can also see the raw argument values, but the socket address `connect` takes is a pointer into the process's memory, and a filter can't follow a pointer. So "connect, but only to localhost" is a rule seccomp can't express. Hold that thought; the next two labs exist because of it.

Let's switch tactics and deny the read instead. `openat` is how everything opens files, so we can't refuse it wholesale either, but we can change what a refusal looks like. `--action kill` swaps `ERRNO` for `KILL_PROCESS`:

```bash
uv run python seccomp_sandbox.py --deny openat --action kill -- cat decoys/.aws/credentials || echo "exit=$?"
```

```console
exit=159
```

The process is gone before the syscall runs. That's `SIGSYS`, signal 31, which the shell reports as exit 159 (128 plus the signal number), with the core-dump notice an interactive shell prints for any child a signal killed. Which verdict to use is a real design choice: `ERRNO` lets a program notice and continue, which is what you want for a tool that has a fallback; `KILL_PROCESS` is what you want when a call happening at all means something has gone badly wrong.

Question: our filter denied `connect`, and goose died. Why didn't the `openat` and `execve` calls before it fail too?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

Because the filter is an allowlist with one exception. Instruction 05 is `ret ALLOW`, and every syscall number that isn't 42 falls through to it. Docker's default profile is the other way round: a default of `ERRNO` and a long list of exceptions that return `ALLOW`. Both shapes are just the order of the `jeq` lines and which `ret` comes last, and you'll build the second shape in the next section.

</details>

## The same agent, in a container

_~8 min · Hands-on_

Docker applies a seccomp profile to every container by default. It's an allowlist in JSON, [maintained in the moby project](https://github.com/moby/profiles/blob/main/seccomp/default.json), with `defaultAction: SCMP_ACT_ERRNO` and a few hundred named exceptions, and the [Docker docs](https://docs.docker.com/engine/security/seccomp/) put the count of blocked calls at around 44 of 300-odd. What it blocks is the interesting part: `mount`, `reboot`, `kexec_load`, `ptrace` of other processes, `bpf`, `unshare` with new user namespaces. Calls a normal program never makes and an escape attempt usually does.

Let's build the agent's image. It's based on Rocky Linux 8, the same userland as this machine, and that's deliberate: the profile we're about to generate comes from a trace taken on this host, and a container with a newer C library reaches for syscalls (`clone3`, `rseq`) that the trace never saw. The build fetches from the internet, and on the sandbox Docker's build network can't, so it runs on the host's network:

```bash
docker build --network=host -t agent-box .
```

```console
$ docker build --network=host -t agent-box .
```

The container reaches Ollama on the host, so it runs with the host's network too. First with Docker's default profile, which is what you get when you say nothing:

```bash
docker run --rm --network host agent-box 2>&1 | tail -8
```

```console
$ docker run --rm --network host agent-box 2>&1 | tail -8
```

It works, same as on the host, because nothing the agent does is on Docker's block list. Now let's build a profile from what we observed instead. `profile_from_strace.py` reads the `strace -c` summary from earlier and emits a profile that allows exactly those calls plus the handful a container's own startup makes:

```bash
uv run python profile_from_strace.py agent.strace > agent-seccomp.json
head -12 agent-seccomp.json
```

```console
$ uv run python profile_from_strace.py agent.strace > agent-seccomp.json
$ head -12 agent-seccomp.json
{
  "defaultAction": "SCMP_ACT_ERRNO",
  "defaultErrnoRet": 1,
  "architectures": [
    "SCMP_ARCH_X86_64"
  ],
  "syscalls": [
    {
      "names": [
        "access",
        "arch_prctl",
        "bind",
```

Run the agent under it:

```bash
docker run --rm --network host --security-opt seccomp=agent-seccomp.json agent-box 2>&1 | tail -8
```

```console
$ docker run --rm --network host --security-opt seccomp=agent-seccomp.json agent-box 2>&1 | tail -8
```

That one works too, because it's the same agent doing the same task. Now run one command the trace never contained. The image's entrypoint is the agent, so this bypasses it and hands the container a shell directly:

```bash
docker run --rm --security-opt seccomp=agent-seccomp.json --entrypoint /bin/sh agent-box \
  -c 'mkdir -p build && chmod 700 build && ls -ld build'
```

```console
chmod: changing permissions of 'build': Operation not permitted
```

`chmod: changing permissions of 'build': Operation not permitted`. The first run never called `chmod`, so `chmod` isn't in the allowlist, so it fails with `EPERM`. A profile generated from one observed run allows one observed run. That's the tension every syscall allowlist lives with: tight enough to matter means a new library version, a new tool, or a model that phrases a command differently trips it, and loose enough never to trip it means it stops mattering. Docker's default profile is where years of that judgement landed, which is why the docs tell you not to replace it casually.

<details>
<summary>Where this lives in Kubernetes</summary>

The same JSON, set per pod or per container under `securityContext.seccompProfile`. `type: RuntimeDefault` is the runtime's own profile, the one you just ran without flags, and `type: Localhost` points at a file on the node. Kubernetes has applied `RuntimeDefault` by default since it went stable, so a pod with no `seccompProfile` at all is already running under roughly what you saw here.

</details>

Compare `--security-opt seccomp=unconfined` if you want to see the agent run with no filter at all. Nothing visible changes, which is the point: seccomp only ever shows up when it says no.
